free_tier.stated: No documented per-gem size limit and no documented total quota — this is itself the finding: RubyGems publishes its rate limits and its acceptable-use policy but NOT a byte limit. Per-gem size is exposed per version via the API; large gems (e.g. binaries) do get 413'd in practice.
free_tier.notes: the headline offer as the seed recorded it; the binding constraint is in limits[]

per_object_cap.stated: no per-object cap was extracted from the seed's quota and limits prose; absence here is a gap in this conversion, not a vendor claim that no cap exists
per_object_cap.notes: extraction found no per-object clause; some of these providers meter on object count rather than bytes, and some state no cap

retention.stated: No published per-gem byte cap (I could not find one in the docs, the acceptable-use policy, or the server source). Version strings and gem names are permanent.

egress.terms: Free and unmetered, Cloudflare-fronted. Probe: GET https://rubygems.org/downloads/rails-7.0.0.gem -> 200, Server: cloudflare, Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, Accept-Ranges: bytes.

tooling: POST /api/v1/gems with the .gem body (gem push); GET /downloads/<name>-<ver>.gem or /gems/<name>-<ver>.gem. First-class clients (gem push, bundler). Rate-limit config is public in the repo (rack_attack.rb: PUSH_LIMIT = 400 per 60 minutes).
chaining: 400 pushes/hour is the most generous publish rate in the entire niche — 9,600 gems/day, i.e. ~2-9 TB/day if each gem were at a hypothetical 250 MB. If the undocumented size limit is anywhere near npm's, RubyGems becomes the highest-throughput package-registry store found. Confirm the size cap before relying on it.
limits_note: 400 push requests/hour/IP; 300/5min and 600/25h on *failed* pushes; 10 yanks/10min. No published per-gem byte cap (I could not find one in the docs, the acceptable-use policy, or the server source). Version strings and gem names are permanent.
